claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has high strength but limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Sharp internal interfaces cause dislocation pile-ups in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation accumulation at sharp internal boundaries produces local stress concentrations and early microcracking.
A controlled post-solidification annealing treatment below the solvus temperature will induce a complexion transition at the internal lamellar interfaces.
Annealing permits minor diffusion and elemental segregation at the interfaces.
Diffusion and segregation transform sharp, brittle interfaces into more diffuse and ductile complexion-type boundaries.
The modified interfaces can act as dislocation sinks and absorb dislocations.
Dislocation absorption at the modified interfaces reduces local stress concentrations from pile-ups.
Reduced local stress concentrations delay microcracking during tensile deformation.
Annealing will increase room-temperature engineering strain at fracture relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Retention of the overall dual-phase architecture sustains or improves strength after annealing.
Excessive grain growth or dissolution of the lamellar microstructure would prevent the proposed beneficial response.
